source_refs.note: Topic printed as 2.4.1, printed page 26: emission and absorption spectra (Figures 2.2 and 2.3).

blocks.title: Atomic emission spectrum
blocks.text: When an element in its gaseous state is heated to high temperatures or subjected to electrical discharge, radiation of certain wavelengths is emitted. The spectrum of this radiation contains coloured lines and is called atomic emission spectrum.
The atomic emission spectrum of hydrogen is shown in Figure 2.2 (a).

blocks.title: Atomic absorption spectrum
blocks.text: When a beam of white light is passed through a gaseous sample of an element in cold state, certain wavelengths are absorbed. The wavelengths of the white light that has been absorbed by the atoms show up as dark lines on the spectrum. The spectrum of this radiation is called an atomic absorption spectrum.

The atomic absorption spectrum of hydrogen is shown in Figure 2.2 (b). The wavelengths of the dark lines in the absorption spectrum are exactly the same as those of coloured lines in the emission spectrum.

blocks.alt: (a) The emission spectrum of hydrogen: four coloured lines, violet, blue-violet, blue-green and red, on a dark grey strip. (b) The absorption spectrum of hydrogen: a continuous rainbow from violet to red crossed by four dark lines at the same places. A scale below runs from 400 nm to 700 nm.
blocks.caption: Figure 2.2: (a) atomic emission spectrum of hydrogen (b) atomic absorption spectrum of hydrogen (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 2.2).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: In the printed Figure 2.2 the lines do not sit at their wavelengths on the figure's own 400-700 nm scale (the red line is near 620 nm). The visible hydrogen lines are at 410, 434, 486 and 656 nm, as drawn above.

Each element has a unique arrangement of electrons and thus a unique range of fixed energy levels. It follows that the wavelengths and frequencies of the radiation absorbed or emitted when electrons jump from one energy level to another must also be unique. This uniqueness convinces us to conclude that every element has its own characteristic spectrum. Therefore, every element is identified by its characteristic spectrum. Hence, we can say that atomic spectra are the finger prints of the elements. Figure 2.3 shows the emission spectra of some elements.

blocks.alt: Emission line patterns of hydrogen, helium, neon, sodium and mercury, each a grey strip with coloured lines, red on the left. The hydrogen lines are marked 656 nm, 486 nm, 434 nm and 410 nm.
blocks.caption: Figure 2.3: Spectral series of various elements as plotted by a spectrometer (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 2.3).
